puzzles.title: barcode decoding
puzzles.layTitle: Reading DNA name tags full of typos
puzzles.laySummary: Scientists can attach tiny DNA “name tags”, called barcodes, to molecules so they can later tell where each one came from. In spatial transcriptomics, every spot on a glass slide gets its own barcode, revealing where a gene was active in a tissue. The problem: the printer that makes these barcodes is sloppy, and up to one in five DNA letters ends up wrong, missing or extra. CRIG researchers tested three computer programs that try to recognize the right barcode despite these errors. The program QUIK came out on top: it was by far the fastest and correctly identified the most barcodes. Longer barcodes (34 to 36 letters) also made decoding much more reliable. The CRIGram is inspired by Figure 3B.

source.article: Benchmarking DNA barcode decoding strategies under high error rates

puzzles.title: ferroptosis-armed DC vaccine
puzzles.layTitle: Training the immune system to fight brain tumours
puzzles.laySummary: Gliomas are aggressive brain tumors that are hard to treat, partly because the immune system barely notices them. CRIG researchers tested a vaccine made from dendritic cells, the “scouts” of the immune system. They fed these cells with the remains of glioma cells killed by ferroptosis, a type of cell death driven by iron. In mice, the vaccine slowed tumor growth, helped them live longer, and some never developed a tumor at all. It also drew more killer T cells into the tumor and built lasting immune memory. Two alarm signals released by the dying cells, calreticulin and ATP, proved essential. The CRIGram is inspired by Figure 5a.

source.article: Ferroptosis-armed dendritic cell vaccines for glioma immunotherapy

puzzles.title: EV cargo
puzzles.layTitle: Tiny cell parcels that tell the story of cancer
puzzles.laySummary: Almost every cell in our body releases tiny bubbles called extracellular vesicles. Each one carries a sample of the cell’s contents: DNA, RNA, proteins, fats and other small molecules. Tumors release more than healthy tissue, so collecting these bubbles from blood, urine, or spinal fluid could reveal a lot about cancer without surgery. In this review, CRIG researchers describe how scientists study several molecule types at once, an approach called multi-omics. Most studies combine proteins and RNA. The authors also flag the hurdles: isolation methods vary, samples are often tiny, and there is no agreed way to combine the data yet.

source.article: Multi-omics analysis of extracellular vesicle cargo in cancer
